Sampled HR/Recall@10 can reverse model rankings relative to full-catalog evaluation, even in expectation; repeating negative samples reduces sampling uncertainty but cannot remove systematic bias. Small candidate sets increasingly reflect pairwise discrimination, so larger positive–negative margins do not establish better top-10 retrieval. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) demonstrate this formally. [RecSys 2025 research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) examines sampling reliability through resolution, fidelity, robustness and predictive power, using bootstrap confidence intervals and distinguishing full logged-data evaluation from fully observed preferences.

Practical implication for this search: retain fixed host macro validation HR@10 as the selection criterion. On training-history diagnostic targets, reuse identical candidate draws across model comparisons, repeat draws to measure sensitivity, and separately report full-catalog ranks. Stratify by training-derived target popularity and available history length; report stratum sizes and paired changes to expose easy-negative gains or improvements concentrated in popular items. Bootstrap users within each category, preserving model pairing, then recompute the equal-weight four-category macro difference. With one relevant target per user, HR@10 equals Recall@10 for the same candidate set.

Treat margin and context-sensitivity measures as hypotheses requiring empirical validation: compare their changes against host HR@10 changes across tried configurations, reporting category-specific agreement and uncertainty. Distinguish candidate-sampling variability from user-sampling uncertainty. Neither cited study establishes these probes as reliable predictors for GRU4Rec on these four datasets; training-only full-catalog diagnostics also do not establish generalization. Use the evidence to revise one independently trained GRU4Rec model per category, without score fusion or evaluator changes.
